entries.title: A p-value defined without 'or more extreme', and the 0.05 cut-off taught as its meaning
entries.correct_statement: The p-value is the probability, computed under the null hypothesis and the model's assumptions, of a summary statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and no conclusion should rest on whether it crosses a threshold such as 0.05.

citation.source: Wasserstein & Lazar (2016), The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose, The American Statistician 70(2), principles 2 and 3
citation.quote: the probability under a specified statistical model that a statistical summary of the data ... would be equal to or more extreme than its observed value

positive: Probabilidad de observar el resultado si la hipótesis nula es cierta. <0.05 típicamente "significativo".
negative: El valor p es la probabilidad de observar una diferencia al menos tan grande como la tuya **si el tratamiento no tuviera ningún efecto**.

Probabilidad, si la hipótesis nula fuera cierta, de obtener un resultado al menos tan extremo como el observado. No es la probabilidad de que H0 sea cierta, y 0.05 es una convención, no su significado.

entries.title: The bootstrap presented as the fix for small samples or heavy tails
entries.correct_statement: The percentile bootstrap does not rescue a small sample: its intervals are too narrow when n is small (they cover less than the nominal level), and for skewed data it is less accurate than the t interval up to roughly n = 34. The bootstrap shows an estimator's spread and asymmetry without a formula; a small n is a limit that no interval removes.

citation.source: Hesterberg (2015), What Teachers Should Know About the Bootstrap, The American Statistician 69(4), section on narrowness bias
citation.quote: the bootstrap percentile interval ... is less accurate than the t interval for n <= 34

entries.title: `python -m` presented as avoiding sys.path or the working directory
entries.correct_statement: `python -m pkg` finds the module by its import name on sys.path, the same way `import` does, and runs it as part of its package, so relative imports work. It adds the current directory to the start of sys.path, so it depends on the working directory more, not less; that is why the src layout matters.

citation.source: Python 3.12 documentation, Command line and environment, option -m
citation.quote: As with the -c option, the current directory will be added to the start of sys.path.

positive: Ejecutar `python -m familiarity_core` corre el paquete sin pelear con `sys.path` (la lista interna que decide de qué carpetas importar).
Ejecutar `python -m familiarity_core` usa el paquete como __main__ sin pelear con sys.path.
El label es solo UI; la política se decide por un kind tipificado. `python -m familiarity_core` evita pelear con `sys.path`.
python -m usa el paquete instalado/namespace correcto; reduce imports frágiles por cwd
`python -m` usa la entrada del paquete y evita depender del `cwd`
`-m` ejecuta `__main__.py` desde el paquete y evita imports frágiles ligados al `cwd`.
negative: Sin src, ejecutar desde la raíz importa la carpeta local y no el paquete instalado; el fallo aparece solo en otra máquina.
El paquete debe instalarse en el mismo intérprete que ejecuta el script. `python -m pip` dentro del `.venv` evita instalar en otro Python.
`python -m` no evita depender del cwd: lo pone primero en sys.path.

entries.title: A circular import said to break the package unconditionally
entries.correct_statement: Two modules may import each other. It fails only when one uses, while the other is still being initialized, a name the other has not defined yet: a top-level `from b import x` then raises ImportError (cannot import name), and a top-level `b.x` raises AttributeError; both messages name a partially initialized module. A name the other module defined before the cycle was entered works, and so does a plain `import b` with the name used later, inside functions. Extracting the shared code to a third module is still the first remedy.

citation.source: Python 3.12 documentation, Programming FAQ, How can I have modules that mutually import each other?
citation.quote: The problem is that the interpreter will perform the following steps

positive: Los **imports circulares** (módulo A importa a B y B importa a A: Python se enreda) se rompen extrayendo un tercer módulo compartido
- **Contexto:** si `module_a` y `module_b` se necesitan mutuamente, el import circular rompe el paquete al arrancar.
El paquete falla al arrancar por el import circular
Un ciclo A↔B rompe el arranque; el primer recurso es extraer la lógica compartida a un tercer módulo.
negative: Un import circular falla solo cuando un módulo usa un nombre del otro mientras ese otro aún se está cargando; con `import b` y el uso dentro de funciones, funciona.

entries.title: INFO presented as a safe default log level
entries.correct_statement: Unconfigured, Python's root logger shows WARNING and above; INFO is a level a project chooses. The level controls volume, not privacy: personal data is masked or left out of the message at every level, DEBUG included (in Spanish, "enmascarar" or "omitir"; "redactar" means to write).

citation.source: Python 3.12 documentation, Logging HOWTO, When to use logging
citation.quote: The default level is WARNING, which means that only events of this severity and higher will be tracked

positive: Defaults seguros (log level INFO, no debug con PII — *Personally Identifiable Information*, datos personales identificables).
negative: def resolve_log_level(default="INFO", env=None, flag=None) -> str:
Si el flag no se pasó (None), gana env — no inventes un default INFO aquí.
INFO es el nivel que este proyecto elige; sin configurar, Python solo muestra WARNING y superiores.

entries.title: Correlation defined without 'linear'
entries.correct_statement: Pearson's correlation coefficient measures linear association, from -1 to 1. A strong curved relationship can give a value near 0, and correlation does not imply causation.

citation.quote: The Pearson correlation coefficient measures the linear relationship between two datasets.

positive: Relación entre dos variables. -1 a 1. np.corrcoef, df.corr(). Cuidado: correlación no implica causalidad.
negative: Mide la fuerza de la relación lineal entre dos variables, de -1 a 1. Una relación curva puede dar cerca de 0.

entries.title: The 80/20 train/test split taught as the definition
entries.correct_statement: A train/test split holds out data the model never sees while fitting, to estimate performance on new data. The proportion is a choice, not part of the definition: scikit-learn's own default puts 25% in the test set.

citation.quote: If None, the value is set to the complement of the train size. If train_size is also None, it will be set to 0.25.

positive: Dividir datos en entrenamiento (80%) y prueba (20%). El modelo nunca "ve" el test durante training.
negative: Separar los datos en entrenamiento y prueba antes de ajustar nada; la proporción (por ejemplo 80/20 o 75/25) se elige, no viene dada.

entries.title: ROC-AUC called robust to class imbalance
entries.correct_statement: ROC-AUC does not change when the class proportions change. That is why it can stay high while the rare class is predicted badly; with imbalanced classes, read precision-recall (average precision) beside it.

citation.source: Fawcett (2006), An introduction to ROC analysis, Pattern Recognition Letters 27(8), section 9; Saito & Rehmsmeier (2015), PLOS ONE 10(3) e0118432
citation.quote: one of the attractions of ROC graphs, namely that they are insensitive to class skew (Fawcett 2006)

positive: Área bajo curva ROC. Métrica para clasificación binaria. 0.5 = azar, 1.0 = perfecto. Robusta a desbalance.
negative: No cambia si cambia la proporción de clases; por eso puede verse alta aunque la clase rara se prediga mal. Con clases desbalanceadas, mira también la curva precisión-recall.

entries.title: StratifiedKFold called obligatory for classification
entries.correct_statement: StratifiedKFold keeps the class proportions in each fold and is the usual choice for classification - scikit-learn already uses it when cv is an integer and the estimator is a classifier. It is the wrong choice for grouped or time-ordered data (GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit).

citation.quote: For integer/None inputs, if classifier is True and y is either binary or multiclass, StratifiedKFold is used.

positive: KFold que mantiene proporción de clases en cada fold. Obligatorio para clasificación desbalanceada.
negative: KFold que mantiene la proporción de clases en cada fold. Es la opción habitual en clasificación; con grupos o datos en el tiempo se usa GroupKFold o TimeSeriesSplit.

entries.title: A UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY column given its own CREATE INDEX, as if the constraint left it unindexed
entries.correct_statement: In SQLite a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint is implemented by a unique index the engine creates itself (sqlite_autoindex_<table>_N; an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the rowid), so a lookup on that column is already a search, not a full scan. A second CREATE INDEX on that one column gives queries nothing the automatic index does not, and every write must maintain both. CREATE INDEX helps a column with no index: a repeated foreign key such as evidence.entity_id, or document_id in a table that does not declare it UNIQUE (exercise S12-T3-B-E3). NOT NULL creates no index.

citation.source: SQLite documentation, CREATE TABLE, UNIQUE constraints
citation.quote: In most cases, UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints are implemented by creating a unique index in the database.

positive: con.execute("CREATE TABLE clients (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, document_id TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL)"); con.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_doc ON clients(document_id)")
CREATE TABLE clients(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, document_id TEXT, UNIQUE(document_id)); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_doc ON clients(document_id);
CREATE TABLE clients(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE INDEX idx_id ON clients(id)
negative: con.execute("CREATE TABLE clients(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, document_id TEXT)"); con.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_document_id ON clients(document_id)")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE clients (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, document_id TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL)")
CREATE TABLE evidence(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, entity_id TEXT, kind TEXT UNIQUE); CREATE INDEX idx_entity ON evidence(entity_id)
CREATE TABLE clients(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, document_id TEXT UNIQUE, name TEXT); CREATE INDEX idx_doc_name ON clients(document_id, name)
`UNIQUE` ya crea un índice (`sqlite_autoindex_clients_2`), así que `CREATE INDEX` sobre `document_id` sobraría; en E3 la columna no es `UNIQUE` y ahí sí creas `idx_document_id`.

entries.title: `Connection.row_factory` presented as what makes `:name` placeholders work
entries.correct_statement: A named placeholder (`:name`) takes its values from a dict whose keys name every placeholder; a `?` placeholder takes them from a sequence such as a tuple, by position. `Connection.row_factory` plays no part in binding: it decides the shape of the rows a query returns (a tuple by default, `sqlite3.Row` to read columns by name). A sequence passed to named placeholders emits DeprecationWarning in Python 3.12 and raises ProgrammingError from 3.14.

citation.source: Python 3.12 documentation, sqlite3, How to use placeholders to bind values in SQL queries; Connection.row_factory; Cursor.execute
citation.quote: For the named style, parameters must be an instance of a dict (or a subclass), which must contain keys for all named parameters; any extra items are ignored.

positive: Usa placeholders `?` (o `:name` con `Connection.row_factory`).
Para parámetros con nombre (`:cid`) necesitas configurar `con.row_factory`.
`row_factory` habilita los placeholders `:name` en la consulta.
negative: Usa placeholders `?` con una tupla, o `:name` con un dict de parámetros.
Los placeholders `:name` toman un dict; `row_factory` no interviene: solo decide la forma de las filas que salen de la consulta.
`:name` no necesita `row_factory`; toma un dict.
Con `con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row` cada fila permite leer columnas con nombre, como `fila["document_id"]`.
